## 1) Introduction
Crop production and harvest is an area of study whose output affects every general population. This is becuase everyone, regardless of their different facets of life, needs to consume food to survive. With the growing trend of global temperature, food production and harvest quantity may fluctuate. 

This study aims answer question about the effects of heat treatment to cranberries and result we observe in production of cranberries. 

We aim of answer the following questions : 

1. How does heat stress affect yield as measured by the total weight of fruit?
2. How does heat stress affect yield as measured by the total weight of healthy fruit?
3. How does heat stress affect yield as measured by the percentage of healthy berries by count?
4. How does heat stress affect yield as measured by the percentage of healthy fruit by weight?
5. How do the cultivars, years, and intensity of the heat shocks (in the case of the acute heat stress experiment) affect the various measures of yield?


## 2) Data and Experimental Design

```{r data-setup, include=FALSE}
data_raw <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wwy200311gy-sudo/stat628/refs/heads/main/src/acute_yield_data_fall_2026.csv")

data <- data_raw %>%
  mutate(
    year = factor(year),
    cultivar = factor(toupper(trimws(cultivar))),
    intensity_group = factor(toupper(trimws(intensity_group)),
                             levels = c("D", "C", "B", "A")),
    treatment = factor(toupper(trimws(treatment)),
                       levels = c("CONTROL", "OTC"),
                       labels = c("Control", "OTC")),
    heat_group = factor(ifelse(treatment == "Control", "Control",
                               as.character(intensity_group)),
                        levels = c("Control", "D", "C", "B", "A")),
    pair_id = interaction(year, cultivar, intensity_group, plot, drop = TRUE),
    total_weight = healthy_weight + rotten_weight,
    healthy_count_pct = 100 * (healthy_n / (healthy_n + rotten_n)),
    healthy_weight_prop = healthy_weight / total_weight,
    healthy_weight_pct = 100 * healthy_weight_prop,
    pulses = as.numeric(c(A = 4, B = 3, C = 2, D = 1)[as.character(intensity_group)])
  )

# Plain-language labels used in figures and tables
eda_group_labels    <- c(Control = "Control", D = "1 pulse", C = "2 pulses",
                         B = "3 pulses", A = "4 pulses")
eda_cultivar_labels <- c(MQ = "Mullica Queen", ST = "Stevens")
```

```{r design-checks, include=FALSE}
# Design checks: 96 plots, 48 pairs, each pair has one Control and one heated plot
stopifnot(nrow(data) == 96, nlevels(data$pair_id) == 48)
stopifnot(!anyNA(data$heat_group))
stopifnot(all(data %>% count(pair_id) %>% pull(n) == 2))
stopifnot(all(data %>%
  group_by(pair_id) %>%
  summarise(ok = setequal(as.character(treatment), c("Control", "OTC")),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  pull(ok)))
stopifnot(all(data$total_weight > 0),
          all(data$healthy_n + data$rotten_n > 0),
          all(data$healthy_weight > 0))

eda_n_missing    <- sum(is.na(data_raw))
eda_pairs_per_cell <- unique(as.vector(table(
  data$cultivar[data$treatment == "OTC"],
  data$year[data$treatment == "OTC"],
  data$intensity_group[data$treatment == "OTC"])))

# Correlations between the yield measures
eda_cor_weight <- cor(data$total_weight, data$healthy_weight)
eda_cor_pct    <- cor(data$healthy_count_pct, data$healthy_weight_pct)
```

**Experimental design.** The data contain `r nrow(data)` plots of two cranberry
cultivars, Mullica Queen and Stevens, each grown in its own field, in 2024 and
2025. The plots form `r nlevels(data$pair_id)` pairs of neighbouring plots: in
each pair, one plot was heated and the other was left unheated as a Control.
Heated plots received 1, 2, 3 or 4 heat pulses (intensity groups D, C, B and A
in the data), with `r eda_pairs_per_cell` pairs for each number of pulses in
every combination of cultivar and year. All Control plots received the same
treatment, whatever happened to their paired heated plot, so we treat the 12
Control plots of each cultivar and year as one Control group. The heat treatment
therefore has five levels: Control and 1, 2, 3 or 4 pulses.

**Yield measures.** For each plot, the data record the number and weight of
healthy and rotten berries. From these we calculated the four measures of yield
studied in this report: total fruit weight (healthy plus rotten weight), healthy
fruit weight, the percentage of healthy berries by count, and the percentage of
healthy fruit by weight.

**Data checks.** The data have no missing values. Every pair
contains exactly one Control and one heated plot, and all weights and berry
counts are positive. No observations were removed, so all analyses use the full
`r nrow(data)` plots.

```{r design-pairs-cor, include=FALSE}
# Correlation between the two plots of a pair (log total weight)
st_wide <- data %>%
  select(pair_id, cultivar, year, treatment, total_weight) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = treatment, values_from = total_weight)

st_cor_all <- cor(log(st_wide$Control), log(st_wide$OTC))
st_cor_within <- st_wide %>%
  group_by(cultivar, year) %>%
  summarise(r = cor(log(Control), log(OTC)), .groups = "drop")
```

**Paired design.** The two plots of a pair are neighbours and share soil and
growing conditions, so their yields are not independent. All models in this
report therefore include a random effect for each pair, which allows each pair
to have its own baseline yield.

**First look at the data.** Control yields were similar in three of the four
combinations of cultivar and year, but Stevens produced only about a third as
much fruit in 2025 (see the table below). To put all plots on a common
scale, the figure below expresses each plot as a percentage of the mean
Control value of its own cultivar and year, with both cultivars shown together.
Most heated groups had a lower average yield than Control. For the two weights,
the clearest reductions occurred with three or four pulses in 2025, whereas in
2024 there was no clear pattern with the number of pulses. For the two
percentages, the share of healthy fruit was lower in every heated group, by a
broadly similar amount whatever the number of pulses. Plots varied widely
within each group, and many heated plots overlapped with Control plots, so the
models in Sections 3 to 6 are needed to judge which differences are reliable.

```{r eda-control-table}
data %>%
  filter(treatment == "Control") %>%
  group_by(cultivar, year) %>%
  summarise(
    `Total (g)`            = round(mean(total_weight)),
    `Healthy (g)`          = round(mean(healthy_weight)),
    `Healthy, % by count`  = round(mean(healthy_count_pct), 1),
    `Healthy, % by weight` = round(mean(healthy_weight_pct), 1),
    .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(cultivar = eda_cultivar_labels[as.character(cultivar)]) %>%
  rename(Cultivar = cultivar, Year = year) %>%
  kable(caption = "Mean of each yield measure in the Control plots, by cultivar and year.")
```

```{r eda-overview, fig.cap="Each yield measure as a percentage of the mean of the Control plots of the same cultivar and year, with both cultivars combined. Small points are individual plots; diamonds joined by lines are group means, coloured by year. The dashed line at 100 marks the Control level. Vertical scales differ between panels."}
eda_long <- data %>%
  select(cultivar, year, treatment, heat_group,
         total_weight, healthy_weight, healthy_count_pct, healthy_weight_pct) %>%
  pivot_longer(c(total_weight, healthy_weight, healthy_count_pct, healthy_weight_pct),
               names_to = "measure", values_to = "value") %>%
  group_by(measure, cultivar, year) %>%
  mutate(rel = 100 * value / mean(value[treatment == "Control"])) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
    measure = factor(measure,
      levels = c("total_weight", "healthy_weight",
                 "healthy_count_pct", "healthy_weight_pct"),
      labels = c("Total fruit weight", "Healthy fruit weight",
                 "Healthy berries (% by count)", "Healthy fruit (% by weight)")),
    heat_group = factor(heat_group, levels = names(eda_group_labels),
                        labels = eda_group_labels))

ggplot(eda_long, aes(x = heat_group, y = rel, colour = year, group = year)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 100, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.15, dodge.width = 0.6),
             alpha = 0.5, size = 1.2) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "line", position = position_dodge(width = 0.6)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 18, size = 3,
               position = position_dodge(width = 0.6)) +
  facet_wrap(~ measure, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Percent of mean Control value", colour = "Year") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 9) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))
```

## 3) How does heat stress affect yield as measured by the total weight of fruit?

Appendix A compares the candidate models for total weight. The fitted model has heat group by year, cultivar, and the cultivar-by-year shift in its fixed part, a random intercept for each pair, and separate residual variances for Control and heated plots.

```{r tw-fit, include=FALSE}
# Final model: H2 fixed effects with separate residual variances for Control
# and OTC plots. The comparison that leads to this choice is in Appendix A.
tw_final <- lme(log(total_weight) ~ heat_group * year + cultivar + year:cultivar,
                random = ~ 1 | pair_id, data = data, method = "REML")
tw_final <- update(tw_final, weights = varIdent(form = ~ 1 | treatment))

tw_sd_pair <- as.numeric(VarCorr(tw_final)["(Intercept)", "StdDev"])
tw_sd_ctrl <- sigma(tw_final)
tw_sd_otc  <- tw_sd_ctrl * coef(tw_final$modelStruct$varStruct, unconstrained = FALSE)[1]
```

### 3.1 Final model

The final model for plot $i$ is

$$
\log(Y_i) = \mu + \alpha_{g(i)} + \beta_{t(i)} + (\alpha\beta)_{g(i)\,t(i)} + \gamma_{c(i)} + (\beta\gamma)_{t(i)\,c(i)} + b_{k(i)} + \varepsilon_i,
$$

where $Y_i$ is the total fruit weight in grams and $\log$ is the natural logarithm. $\mu$ is the overall intercept, $\alpha_{g}$ the effect of heat group $g$, $\beta_{t}$ the effect of year $t$, $\gamma_{c}$ the effect of cultivar $c$, $(\alpha\beta)_{gt}$ the heat-by-year interaction, and $(\beta\gamma)_{tc}$ the cultivar-by-year shift. $b_{k}$ is the random intercept of pair $k$, with $b_k \sim N(0, \sigma_b^2)$, and $\varepsilon_i$ is the residual error, with variance $\sigma^2_{\text{Control}}$ in Control plots and $\sigma^2_{\text{Heated}}$ in heated plots. The estimated standard deviations are $\hat\sigma_b = `r round(tw_sd_pair, 3)`$, $\hat\sigma_{\text{Control}} = `r round(tw_sd_ctrl, 3)`$ and $\hat\sigma_{\text{Heated}} = `r round(tw_sd_otc, 3)`$. The model was fitted by restricted maximum likelihood in R with nlme.


### 3.2 Coefficients of the final model

```{r tw-coef}
tw_coef_tab <- summary(tw_final)$tTable
tw_coef_ci  <- intervals(tw_final, which = "fixed")$fixed

data.frame(
  Term       = rownames(tw_coef_tab),
  Estimate   = tw_coef_tab[, "Value"],
  SE         = tw_coef_tab[, "Std.Error"],
  p_value    = format.pval(tw_coef_tab[, "p-value"], digits = 3, eps = 1e-4),
  Ratio      = exp(tw_coef_tab[, "Value"]),
  Lower_95   = exp(tw_coef_ci[, "lower"]),
  Upper_95   = exp(tw_coef_ci[, "upper"]),
  row.names  = NULL
) %>%
  kable(digits = 3,
        caption = "Fixed-effect estimates of the final heteroscedastic H2 model.")
```

Control, 2024 and Mullica Queen are the reference levels. A `heat_group` coefficient is the log ratio of total weight in that heat group to Control in 2024 for Mullica Queen. A `:year2025` term is the additional change in 2025, `cultivarST` is the Stevens minus Mullica Queen difference in 2024, and `year2025:cultivarST` is the extra 2025 change for Stevens.



### 3.3 Predicted yields

The figure below shows the fitted mean total fruit weight for each heat group, cultivar and year, with 95% confidence intervals. In 2024 the four heat groups sit close to Control. In 2025 the estimate falls from Control to four pulses. Mullica Queen has the higher baseline, so the same proportional fall is the larger loss in grams.

```{r tw-estimates, fig.width=8, fig.height=6, fig.cap="Estimated total fruit weight by heat group, cultivar (rows) and year (columns). Blue points are the means estimated by the final model, joined by lines, with 95% confidence intervals shown as bars; grey points are the individual plots. Control and heated plots are allowed different residual variances, so the intervals of heated plots are wider."}
tw_emm <- emmeans(tw_final, ~ heat_group | year * cultivar, type = "response")
tw_est <- as.data.frame(summary(tw_emm))

set.seed(1)
ggplot() +
  geom_jitter(data = data, aes(x = heat_group, y = total_weight),
              width = 0.12, height = 0, colour = "grey60", alpha = 0.7, size = 1.6) +
  geom_errorbar(data = tw_est, aes(x = heat_group, ymin = lower.CL, ymax = upper.CL),
                width = 0.15, colour = "grey35") +
  geom_line(data = tw_est, aes(x = heat_group, y = response, group = 1),
            colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(data = tw_est, aes(x = heat_group, y = response),
             colour = "steelblue", size = 2.4) +
  facet_grid(cultivar ~ year, labeller = labeller(cultivar = eda_cultivar_labels)) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = eda_group_labels) +
  labs(x = "Heat group", y = "Total fruit weight (g)",
       title = "Estimated total fruit weight by heat group, cultivar and year") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)
```

### 3.4 Answer

Heat stress lowers total fruit weight, and the size of the drop depends on the year and on the number of pulses. Averaged over the four heat groups, heated plots produced about 11.5% less fruit than Control. The reduction was about 7.8% in 2024 and about 15.1% in 2025. Within 2025, four pulses gave about 36.6% less fruit than Control and three pulses about 19.1% less. Across the four heat groups the estimate falls by about 9% for each additional pulse, but the slope is weak in 2024 at about −3% per pulse (p = 0.36) and strong in 2025 at about −15% per pulse (p < 0.001). There is no clear heat-by-cultivar interaction (p = 0.28): Mullica Queen and Stevens differ mainly in their baseline, and the Stevens baseline is much lower in 2025. Control and heated plots were also allowed different residual variances, which the likelihood-ratio test supports, so the estimates above come from that model.

## 4) How does heat stress affect yield as measured by the total weight of healthy fruit?

```{r hw-setup, include=FALSE}
# Plain-language labels used in the figures and tables of this section
hw_group_labels    <- c(Control = "Control", D = "1 pulse", C = "2 pulses",
                        B = "3 pulses", A = "4 pulses")
hw_cultivar_labels <- c(MQ = "Mullica Queen", ST = "Stevens")
```

```{r, include=FALSE}
# Descriptive statistics

# 1a. Mean, SD and n of healthy weight in every cultivar x year x heat group
data %>%
  group_by(year, cultivar, heat_group) %>%
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean = mean(healthy_weight),
            sd   = sd(healthy_weight),
            min  = min(healthy_weight),
            max  = max(healthy_weight),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  print(n = Inf)
```

```{r, include=FALSE}
# 1b. Raw data: every plot as one point, mean +/- SE in red
ggplot(data, aes(x = heat_group, y = healthy_weight)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.12, alpha = 0.6, colour = "grey35") +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se, colour = "red", size = 0.5) +
  facet_grid(cultivar ~ year) +
  labs(x = "Heat group (Control, then D = 1 ... A = 4 pulses)",
       y = "Healthy fruit weight (g)",
       title = "Healthy fruit weight by heat group, cultivar and year",
       subtitle = "Grey = individual plots; red = mean +/- SE") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)
```



```{r, include=FALSE}
# Within-pair ratio of healthy weight
# Keep only the columns that are identical within a pair, plus the ones to spread.
# (Other columns such as rotten_n differ between the two rows and would prevent pivot_wider from merging the pair.)
pairs_wide <- data %>%
  select(pair_id, year, cultivar, intensity_group, pulses, treatment, healthy_weight) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = treatment, values_from = healthy_weight) %>%
  mutate(ratio = OTC / Control,
         log_ratio = log(ratio))

nrow(pairs_wide)

# Summary: geometric mean ratio per cultivar-year-intensity
pairs_wide %>%
  group_by(year, cultivar, intensity_group) %>%
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean_log_ratio = mean(log_ratio),
            geo_mean_ratio = exp(mean_log_ratio),
            .groups = "drop")%>%
  print(n = Inf)

```

### 4.1 First look

**Comparing each heated plot with its own Control.** The figure below shows the ratio of healthy fruit weight between each heated plot and its neighbouring Control plot. In `r sum(pairs_wide$log_ratio < 0)` of the 48 pairs (`r round(100 * mean(pairs_wide$log_ratio < 0))`%), the heated plot produced less healthy fruit than its Control, so heat reduced healthy weight in most pairs. The pattern across heat intensities differed between years. In 2024, the ratios were similar for all four intensities: in most groups, heated plots produced about 15 to 25% less healthy fruit than their Controls, and there was no tendency for more pulses to cause a larger reduction. In 2025, the ratios decreased as the number of heat pulses increased, and heated plots that received three or four pulses produced clearly less healthy fruit than those that received one or two. 

```{r hw-logratio, fig.cap="Ratio of healthy fruit weight in each heated (OTC) plot to that in its paired Control plot, by number of heat pulses, cultivar (rows) and year (columns). Grey points are the 48 individual pairs; red points and bars show the mean and plus or minus one standard error of the log ratios. The dashed line marks a ratio of 1 (no difference); points below it are pairs in which the heated plot produced less healthy fruit than its own Control. The vertical axis is on a logarithmic scale."}
set.seed(1)
pairs_wide %>%
  mutate(pulses_lab   = factor(intensity_group, levels = c("D", "C", "B", "A"),
                               labels = c("1", "2", "3", "4")),
         cultivar_lab = factor(hw_cultivar_labels[as.character(cultivar)],
                               levels = hw_cultivar_labels)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = pulses_lab, y = log_ratio)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, height = 0, alpha = 0.6, colour = "grey35", size = 2) +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se, colour = "red", size = 0.6) +
  facet_grid(cultivar_lab ~ year) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = log(c(0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 1, 1.5)),
                     labels = c("0.3", "0.5", "0.7", "1", "1.5")) +
  labs(x = "Number of heat pulses",
       y = "Healthy weight ratio, heated / Control (log scale)") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)
```

# Numerical version of the same question
grp %>%

```

```{r, include=FALSE}
# Candidate models
fit_lmm <- function(form) lmer(form, data = data, REML = FALSE)

# no heat effect at all (baseline: cultivar x year only)
h_noheat <- fit_lmm(log(healthy_weight) ~ cultivar * year + (1 | pair_id))
# heat effect is the same in every cultivar-year
h0 <- fit_lmm(log(healthy_weight) ~ heat_group + cultivar + year + year:cultivar + (1 | pair_id))
# heat effect depends on cultivar
h1 <- fit_lmm(log(healthy_weight) ~ heat_group * cultivar + year + year:cultivar + (1 | pair_id))
# heat effect depends on year
h2 <- fit_lmm(log(healthy_weight) ~ heat_group * year + cultivar + year:cultivar + (1 | pair_id))
# heat effect depends on cultivar and on year, but no three-way interaction
h3 <- fit_lmm(log(healthy_weight) ~ heat_group * (cultivar + year) + year:cultivar + (1 | pair_id))
# full model: heat effect can differ in every cultivar-year
h_full <- fit_lmm(log(healthy_weight) ~ heat_group * cultivar * year + (1 | pair_id))

models <- list(h_noheat = h_noheat, h0 = h0, h1 = h1, h2 = h2, h3 = h3, h_full = h_full)
```


```{r, include=FALSE}
# AIC / BIC table
hw_aic_tab <- data.frame(
  model = names(models),
  df    = sapply(models, function(m) attr(logLik(m), "df")),
  AIC   = sapply(models, AIC),
  BIC   = sapply(models, BIC)
) %>%
  mutate(dAIC = AIC - min(AIC), dBIC = BIC - min(BIC))
print(hw_aic_tab, row.names = FALSE)
```

sapply(models, isSingular)   # TRUE = pair variance estimated as ~0

```{r, include=FALSE}
# Equal-variance model and diagnostics
hw_lmm <- lmer(log(healthy_weight) ~ heat_group * year + cultivar + year:cultivar +
                 (1 | pair_id), data = data, REML = TRUE)
isSingular(hw_lmm)

# Residual diagnostics for the equal-variance model
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))

# Residuals vs fitted values, coloured by treatment
plot(fitted(hw_lmm), resid(hw_lmm),
     col = ifelse(data$treatment == "OTC", "tomato", "grey30"), pch = 16,
     xlab = "Fitted value (log scale)", ylab = "Residual",
     main = "Residuals vs fitted")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
legend("topleft", legend = c("Control", "OTC"),
       col = c("grey30", "tomato"), pch = 16, bty = "n")

# Normal QQ plot of the residuals
qqnorm(resid(hw_lmm), main = "Normal QQ: residuals", pch = 16, col = "grey30")
qqline(resid(hw_lmm))

# Normal QQ plot of the estimated pair effects
re_pair <- ranef(hw_lmm)$pair_id[, 1]
qqnorm(re_pair, main = "Normal QQ: pair effects", pch = 16, col = "grey30")
qqline(re_pair)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

# Residual SD by treatment
data %>%
  mutate(r = resid(hw_lmm)) %>%
  group_by(treatment) %>%
  summarise(sd_resid = sd(r))
```

```{r, include=FALSE}
# Separate residual variances

# Same fixed and random effects as hw_lmm, refitted with nlme
hw_hom <- lme(log(healthy_weight) ~ heat_group * year + cultivar + year:cultivar,
              random = ~ 1 | pair_id, data = data, method = "REML")

# Control and OTC plots have separate residual variances
hw_het <- update(hw_hom, weights = varIdent(form = ~ 1 | treatment))

# Likelihood-ratio test for unequal residual variances
anova(hw_hom, hw_het)

# Estimated residual SD of Control, and ratio OTC SD / Control SD
sigma(hw_het)
coef(hw_het$modelStruct$varStruct, unconstrained = FALSE)
```

qqline(r_pear)

re_pair <- ranef(hw_het)[, 1]
qqnorm(re_pair, main = "Normal QQ: pair effects", pch = 16, col = "grey30")
qqline(re_pair)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

# Pearson residual SD by treatment
data %>%
  mutate(r = r_pear) %>%
  group_by(treatment) %>%
  summarise(sd_resid = sd(r))

### 4.2 Methods

We modelled the natural logarithm of healthy fruit weight with a linear mixed model. The fixed effects were heat group (Control or 1, 2, 3 or 4 pulses), year, cultivar, the interaction between heat group and year, and the interaction between year and cultivar. The model also included a random effect for each pair of plots and, because heated plots varied more than Control plots, a separate residual variance for heated and Control plots. It was fitted by restricted maximum likelihood with the nlme package in R. On the log scale, each heat effect is a proportional change, so we report it as the ratio of healthy weight in heated plots to that in Control plots, or as the corresponding percentage reduction. Within each year, we compared the average of the four heat groups with Control, compared each heat group with Control, adjusting for multiple comparisons with Dunnett's method, and summarised the effect of intensity as the average change per additional pulse among heated plots. We chose this model by comparing it with simpler and more complex alternatives: allowing the heat effect to differ between years improved the fit, whereas allowing it to differ between cultivars did not. Details of the model, its selection and its checks are given in Appendix B.


```{r, include=FALSE}
# Tests and contrasts
joint_tests(hw_final)

emm_h <- emmeans(hw_final, ~ heat_group | year)
```

```{r, include=FALSE}
# Each intensity vs Control within each year, Dunnett-adjusted, as ratios OTC / Control
ct <- contrast(emm_h, "trt.vs.ctrl", ref = "Control")
summary(ct, type = "response", infer = TRUE)
```


```{r, include=FALSE}
# Average OTC effect over the four intensities within each year
ct_avg <- contrast(emm_h, list("OTC avg vs Control" = c(-1, 1/4, 1/4, 1/4, 1/4)))
summary(ct_avg, type = "response", infer = TRUE)
```


```{r, include=FALSE}
# Estimated means of the four heat groups only (used for the dose-response slope)
emm_otc <- emmeans(hw_final, ~ heat_group | year,
                   at = list(heat_group = c("D", "C", "B", "A")))
    
```


```{r, include=FALSE}
# Multiplicative change in healthy weight per additional heat pulse
slope <- contrast(emm_otc, list("per extra pulse" = c(-3, -1, 1, 3) / 10))
summary(slope, type = "response", infer = TRUE)

# Difference in the dose-response slope between years (exploratory)
pairs(slope, by = NULL)
```

emm_all <- emmeans(hw_final, ~ heat_group)
summary(contrast(emm_all, list("OTC avg vs Control" = c(-1, 1/4, 1/4, 1/4, 1/4))),
        type = "response", infer = TRUE)
```



```{r, include=FALSE}
# Model estimates
emm_cell <- emmeans(hw_final, ~ heat_group | year * cultivar)
est <- as.data.frame(summary(emm_cell, type = "response"))   # response, lower.CL, upper.CL in grams

```

```{r hw-results-numbers, include=FALSE}
# Numbers quoted in the Results text and table

# Helpers: percentage reduction from a ratio, and p-value formatting for tables
hw_pct   <- function(r) round(100 * (1 - r))
hw_fmt_p <- function(p) ifelse(p < 0.001, "< 0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p))

# Contrasts as data frames
hw_ct_avg_df <- as.data.frame(summary(ct_avg, type = "response", infer = TRUE))
hw_ct_df     <- as.data.frame(summary(ct, type = "response", infer = TRUE))
hw_slope_df  <- as.data.frame(summary(slope, type = "response", infer = TRUE))
hw_overall   <- as.data.frame(summary(
  contrast(emm_all, list("OTC avg vs Control" = c(-1, 1/4, 1/4, 1/4, 1/4))),
  type = "response", infer = TRUE))

# Average effect in each year
hw_avg24 <- hw_ct_avg_df[hw_ct_avg_df$year == "2024", ]
hw_avg25 <- hw_ct_avg_df[hw_ct_avg_df$year == "2025", ]

# Individual intensities vs Control
hw_ct24 <- hw_ct_df[hw_ct_df$year == "2024", ]
hw_ct25 <- hw_ct_df[hw_ct_df$year == "2025", ]

# Dose-response slopes
hw_slope24 <- hw_slope_df[hw_slope_df$year == "2024", ]
hw_slope25 <- hw_slope_df[hw_slope_df$year == "2025", ]
hw_slope_diff <- as.data.frame(pairs(slope, by = NULL))
hw_poly   <- as.data.frame(contrast(emm_otc, "poly"))
hw_quad25 <- hw_poly$p.value[hw_poly$contrast == "quadratic" & hw_poly$year == "2025"]

# Overall test of the heat-by-year interaction
hw_jt    <- as.data.frame(joint_tests(hw_final))
hw_jt_hy <- hw_jt[hw_jt$`model term` == "heat_group:year", ]

# Estimated healthy weight in grams for one cultivar, year and heat group
hw_est <- function(g, y, c) est$response[est$heat_group == g & est$year == y & est$cultivar == c]
```

### 4.3 Results

**Overall effect of heat.** Averaged over the four heat groups, both cultivars and both years, heated plots produced `r hw_pct(hw_overall$ratio)`% less healthy fruit than Control plots (95% CI `r hw_pct(hw_overall$upper.CL)`% to `r hw_pct(hw_overall$lower.CL)`%, p `r hw_p(hw_overall$p.value)`). The average reduction was similar in the two years, `r hw_pct(hw_avg24$ratio)`% in 2024 and `r hw_pct(hw_avg25$ratio)`% in 2025.


```{r hw-results-table}
bind_rows(
  hw_ct_avg_df %>%
    transmute(Comparison = "Average of the four heat groups vs Control",
              year, ratio, lower.CL, upper.CL, p.value),
  hw_ct_df %>%
    transmute(Comparison = paste(hw_group_labels[sub(" / Control", "", as.character(contrast))],
                                 "vs Control"),
              year, ratio, lower.CL, upper.CL, p.value),
  hw_slope_df %>%
    transmute(Comparison = "Each additional pulse (from 1 to 4 pulses)",
              year, ratio, lower.CL, upper.CL, p.value)
) %>%
  mutate(Estimate = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f to %.2f)", ratio, lower.CL, upper.CL),
         p        = hw_fmt_p(p.value)) %>%
  select(Comparison, year, Estimate, p) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = c(Estimate, p)) %>%
  select(Comparison, Estimate_2024, p_2024, Estimate_2025, p_2025) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("Comparison", "2024: ratio (95% CI)", "2024: p-value",
                      "2025: ratio (95% CI)", "2025: p-value"),
        caption = "Estimated effect of heat on healthy fruit weight in each year, averaged over the two cultivars. Each estimate is the ratio of healthy weight in heated plots to that in Control plots; a ratio of 0.80 means 20% less healthy fruit. For the individual heat groups, confidence intervals and p-values are adjusted for comparing four heat groups with the same Control using Dunnett's method. The last row is the multiplicative change in healthy weight for each additional heat pulse among heated plots, estimated as a straight-line trend across 1 to 4 pulses.")
```

**Individual heat groups and dose response.** In 2025, the reduction grew with the number of pulses: plots that received three and four pulses produced `r hw_pct(hw_ct25$ratio[hw_ct25$contrast == "B / Control"])`% and `r hw_pct(hw_ct25$ratio[hw_ct25$contrast == "A / Control"])`% less healthy fruit than Control, and each additional pulse reduced healthy weight by about `r hw_pct(hw_slope25$ratio)`% (95% CI `r hw_pct(hw_slope25$upper.CL)`% to `r hw_pct(hw_slope25$lower.CL)`%). The estimated reductions for one and two pulses were smaller (`r hw_pct(hw_ct25$ratio[hw_ct25$contrast == "D / Control"])`% and `r hw_pct(hw_ct25$ratio[hw_ct25$contrast == "C / Control"])`%), and their confidence intervals range from a reduction of about `r hw_pct(min(hw_ct25$lower.CL[hw_ct25$contrast %in% c("D / Control", "C / Control")]))`% to an increase of about `r -hw_pct(max(hw_ct25$upper.CL[hw_ct25$contrast %in% c("D / Control", "C / Control")]))`%. In 2024, every heat group was estimated to produce `r hw_pct(max(hw_ct24$ratio))`% to `r hw_pct(min(hw_ct24$ratio))`% less healthy fruit than Control, with no trend with the number of pulses. None of these differences was statistically discernible on its own, but their confidence intervals range from reductions of up to about `r hw_pct(min(hw_ct24$lower.CL))`% to increases of up to about `r -hw_pct(max(hw_ct24$upper.CL))`%, so reductions of 20% or more remain plausible at every intensity. The two years therefore differ mainly in how the effect depends on the number of pulses, rather than in its average size.

**Cultivars.** There was no evidence that the proportional effect of heat differed between Mullica Queen and Stevens, but because their baselines differ, the same proportional reduction means very different losses in grams. In 2025, for example, four pulses reduced the estimated healthy weight of Mullica Queen from `r round(hw_est("Control", "2025", "MQ"))` g to `r round(hw_est("A", "2025", "MQ"))` g, but that of Stevens only from `r round(hw_est("Control", "2025", "ST"))` g to `r round(hw_est("A", "2025", "ST"))` g.

`

```{r hw-estimates, fig.cap="Estimated healthy fruit weight by heat group, cultivar (rows) and year (columns). Blue points are the means estimated by the final model, joined by lines, with 95% confidence intervals shown as bars; grey points are the individual plots. The model assumes that heat reduces healthy weight by the same proportion in both cultivars, so the estimated curves of the two cultivars have the same shape on a proportional scale."}
set.seed(1)
ggplot() +
  geom_jitter(data = data, aes(x = heat_group, y = healthy_weight),

                width = 0.15, colour = "grey35") +
  geom_line(data = est, aes(x = heat_group, y = response, group = 1),
            colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(data = est, aes(x = heat_group, y = response),
             colour = "steelblue", size = 2.4) +
  facet_grid(cultivar ~ year, labeller = labeller(cultivar = hw_cultivar_labels)) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = hw_group_labels) +
  labs(x = "Heat group", y = "Healthy fruit weight (g)") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)
```


```{r, include=FALSE}
# Sensitivity to extreme plots
# Pearson residuals put Control and OTC plots on the same scale
d_res <- data %>% mutate(r = resid(hw_final, type = "pearson"))
d_res %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(r))) %>%
  select(pair_id, year, cultivar, heat_group, healthy_weight, r) %>%
  head(6)

# The pairs containing the 3 largest residuals (2 pairs) are removed and the model is refitted
out_pairs <- d_res %>% arrange(desc(abs(r))) %>% slice(1:3) %>%
  pull(pair_id) %>% as.character() %>% unique()
d_sub <- data %>% filter(!pair_id %in% out_pairs) %>% droplevels()

h2_sub <- update(hw_final, data = d_sub)

emm_sub <- emmeans(h2_sub, ~ heat_group | year)
summary(contrast(emm_sub, "trt.vs.ctrl", ref = "Control"), type = "response", infer = TRUE)
summary(contrast(emm_sub, list("OTC avg vs Control" = c(-1, 1/4, 1/4, 1/4, 1/4))),
        type = "response", infer = TRUE)

emm_sub_otc <- emmeans(h2_sub, ~ heat_group | year,
                       at = list(heat_group = c("D", "C", "B", "A")))
summary(contrast(emm_sub_otc, list("per extra pulse" = c(-3, -1, 1, 3) / 10)),
        type = "response", infer = TRUE)
```

```{r hw-sensitivity-numbers, include=FALSE}
# Numbers quoted in the sensitivity analysis text
hw_n_removed <- 2 * length(out_pairs)

hw_sub_avg <- as.data.frame(summary(
  contrast(emm_sub, list("OTC avg vs Control" = c(-1, 1/4, 1/4, 1/4, 1/4))),
  type = "response", infer = TRUE))
hw_sub_ct <- as.data.frame(summary(
  contrast(emm_sub, "trt.vs.ctrl", ref = "Control"),
  type = "response", infer = TRUE))
hw_sub_slope <- as.data.frame(summary(
  contrast(emm_sub_otc, list("per extra pulse" = c(-3, -1, 1, 3) / 10)),
  type = "response", infer = TRUE))

hw_sub_avg24   <- hw_sub_avg[hw_sub_avg$year == "2024", ]
hw_sub_avg25   <- hw_sub_avg[hw_sub_avg$year == "2025", ]
hw_sub_ct24    <- hw_sub_ct[hw_sub_ct$year == "2024", ]
hw_sub_ct25    <- hw_sub_ct[hw_sub_ct$year == "2025", ]
hw_sub_slope25 <- hw_sub_slope[hw_sub_slope$year == "2025", ]
```

**Sensitivity to extreme plots.** Removing the two heated plots with unusually low healthy weight made the estimated effects slightly smaller but did not change these conclusions; the only difference was that two heat groups in 2024 became individually statistically discernible, which confirms that the evidence for individual heat groups in 2024 is borderline (Appendix B.5).

### 4.4 Limitations

Only the heat treatment was assigned by the experimenters, so only its effects can be interpreted as causal; each cultivar was grown in a single field, so cultivar differences cannot be separated from field differences, and year differences may reflect weather or other unmeasured conditions. With three pairs per heat group in each cultivar and year, the effects of individual heat groups are estimated imprecisely. The model was chosen after examining the data, so its p-values are likely to be somewhat optimistic. Finally, with only two years of data, we cannot tell whether the dose response seen in 2025 or its absence in 2024 is more typical.


### 4.5 Answer

Heat stress reduced the total weight of healthy fruit by about `r hw_pct(hw_overall$ratio)`% on average (95% CI `r hw_pct(hw_overall$upper.CL)`% to `r hw_pct(hw_overall$lower.CL)`%), with a similar average reduction in 2024 and 2025. The effect of the number of pulses, however, differed between years: in 2025 the reduction grew by about `r hw_pct(hw_slope25$ratio)`% with each additional pulse and reached about `r hw_pct(hw_ct25$ratio[hw_ct25$contrast == "A / Control"])`% with four pulses, whereas in 2024 the number of pulses made little difference. The proportional effect was similar for both cultivars, so losses in grams were larger for Mullica Queen, which has the higher baseline. Because this reduction is larger than that for total fruit weight (Section 3), heat appears to lower healthy weight partly by increasing the share of rotten fruit.






```{r helpers, include=FALSE}
# Helpers shared by the text and the tables
fmt_p     <- function(p) ifelse(p < 0.001, "< 0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p))
fmt_share <- function(x, digits = 1) sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f"), 100 * x)
fewer     <- function(r) round(100 * (1 - r))
hc_pct    <- function(r) round(100 * (1 - r))
group_labels    <- c(Control = "Control", D = "1 pulse", C = "2 pulses",
                     B = "3 pulses", A = "4 pulses")
cultivar_labels <- c(MQ = "Mullica Queen", ST = "Stevens")
```

## 5) How does heat stress affect yield as measured by the percentage of healthy berries by count?

Heat changes both how many berries a plot carries and what share of them is healthy. This section looks at counts. The response is `healthy_n`, the number of healthy berries on a plot, which is a count, so the model is a negative-binomial GLMM with a log link, a random intercept for each pair, and all two-way interactions between heat group, cultivar and year.

### 5.1 Final model

```{r hc-fit, include=FALSE}
hc_add  <- glmmTMB(healthy_n ~ heat_group + cultivar + year + (1 | pair_id),
                   family = nbinom2, data = data)
hc_2way <- glmmTMB(healthy_n ~ (heat_group + cultivar + year)^2 + (1 | pair_id),
                   family = nbinom2, data = data)
hc_3way <- glmmTMB(healthy_n ~ heat_group * cultivar * year + (1 | pair_id),
                   family = nbinom2, data = data)
hc_final <- hc_2way

hc_models <- list("Main effects" = hc_add,
                  "All two-way interactions" = hc_2way,
                  "All three-way interactions" = hc_3way)

hc_lrt <- anova(hc_add, hc_2way, hc_3way)
hc_p_two_way   <- hc_lrt$`Pr(>Chisq)`[2]
hc_p_three_way <- hc_lrt$`Pr(>Chisq)`[3]

hc_jt <- as.data.frame(joint_tests(hc_final))
hc_p_heat    <- hc_jt$p.value[hc_jt$`model term` == "heat_group"]
hc_p_heat_by_cultivar <- hc_jt$p.value[hc_jt$`model term` == "heat_group:cultivar"]
hc_p_heat_by_year     <- hc_jt$p.value[hc_jt$`model term` == "heat_group:year"]
hc_p_cult_by_year     <- hc_jt$p.value[hc_jt$`model term` == "cultivar:year"]
```

The model is

```
healthy_n ~ (heat_group + cultivar + year)^2 + (1 | pair_id)
```

Because the link is logarithmic, a coefficient is a log ratio of expected counts, and `exp(beta)` is the multiplicative change in the expected number of healthy berries against the reference group, which is Control in 2024 for Mullica Queen. A ratio of 0.85 therefore means 15% fewer healthy berries.

### 5.2 Results

```{r hc-contrasts, include=FALSE}
hc_emm <- emmeans(hc_final, ~ heat_group | cultivar * year)

hc_ct <- contrast(hc_emm, method = "trt.vs.ctrl", ref = "Control",
                  adjust = "dunnett")
hc_ct_df <- as.data.frame(summary(hc_ct, type = "response", infer = TRUE))
hc_ct_df$percent_change <- 100 * (hc_ct_df$ratio - 1)

hc_avg_df <- as.data.frame(summary(
  contrast(emmeans(hc_final, ~ heat_group),
           list("OTC avg vs Control" = c(-1, 1/4, 1/4, 1/4, 1/4))),
  type = "response", infer = TRUE))

fewer <- function(r) round(100 * (1 - r))
hc_g  <- function(g, cu, yr) hc_ct_df$ratio[hc_ct_df$contrast == paste(g, "/ Control") &
                                             hc_ct_df$cultivar == cu & hc_ct_df$year == yr]

# Raw share of healthy berries by count, used in the conclusion
hc_raw <- data %>%
  group_by(heat_group) %>%
  summarise(pct = mean(healthy_count_pct), .groups = "drop")
hc_raw_control <- hc_raw$pct[hc_raw$heat_group == "Control"]
hc_raw_heated  <- mean(hc_raw$pct[hc_raw$heat_group != "Control"])
```

Averaged over the four heat groups, both years and both cultivars, heated plots produced `r fewer(hc_avg_df$ratio)`% fewer healthy berries than Control, with a 95% confidence interval from `r fewer(hc_avg_df$asymp.UCL)`% to `r fewer(hc_avg_df$asymp.LCL)`% fewer.

```{r hc-figure, fig.width=7.5, fig.height=4.2, fig.cap="Change in the expected number of healthy berries relative to Control, by heat group, cultivar and year. Negative values are reductions. Bars are 95% confidence intervals from the final negative-binomial model, adjusted for four comparisons with the same Control."}
ggplot(hc_ct_df, aes(x = contrast, y = percent_change)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = (asymp.LCL - 1) * 100, ymax = (asymp.UCL - 1) * 100),
                width = 0.15) +
  facet_grid(year ~ cultivar, labeller = labeller(cultivar = cultivar_labels)) +
  labs(x = "Heat group vs Control",
       y = "Change in expected count (%)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

```{r hc-table}
hc_ct_df %>%
  transmute(Cultivar = cultivar_labels[as.character(cultivar)],
            Year = year,
            Comparison = paste(group_labels[sub(" / Control", "", as.character(contrast))],
                               "vs Control"),
            Ratio = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f to %.2f)", ratio, asymp.LCL, asymp.UCL),
            Change = sprintf("%+.0f%%", percent_change),
            p = fmt_p(p.value)) %>%
  arrange(Cultivar, Year, Comparison) %>%
  kable(format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, position = "H", col.names = c("Cultivar", "Year", "Comparison", "Ratio (95% CI)",
                      "Change in expected count", "p-value"),
        caption = "Effect of each heat group on the expected number of healthy berries, relative to Control, separately for each cultivar and year. Ratios are adjusted for four comparisons with the same Control using Dunnett's method. A ratio of 0.85 means 15% fewer healthy berries.",
        longtable = FALSE)
```

The loss is concentrated in 2025 and in Mullica Queen. Four pulses cut the expected count of Mullica Queen in 2025 to `r sprintf("%.2f", hc_g("A", "MQ", "2025"))` of Control, a fall of `r fewer(hc_g("A", "MQ", "2025"))`%, and three pulses to `r sprintf("%.2f", hc_g("B", "MQ", "2025"))`. In 2024 the four heat groups are closer together, and only two pulses in Mullica Queen reach the 5% level after adjustment.

### 5.3 Answer

Heat stress reduces the number of healthy berries, but the size of the reduction varies with cultivar and year. On average, heated plots produced `r fewer(hc_avg_df$ratio)`% fewer healthy berries than Control, with a 95% confidence interval from `r fewer(hc_avg_df$asymp.UCL)`% to `r fewer(hc_avg_df$asymp.LCL)`% (p `r fmt_p(hc_avg_df$p.value)`). The 2025 season carries most of the loss, reaching `r fewer(hc_g("A", "MQ", "2025"))`% fewer healthy berries with four pulses in Mullica Queen and `r fewer(hc_g("A", "ST", "2025"))`% in Stevens, whereas in 2024 the four heat groups sit closer together.

The joint tests show a clear heat effect, p `r fmt_p(hc_p_heat)`, and a large cultivar-by-year shift, p `r fmt_p(hc_p_cult_by_year)`. The heat effect also differs between years, p = `r fmt_p(hc_p_heat_by_year)`, which is the source of the 2025 losses. It differs less clearly between cultivars, p = `r fmt_p(hc_p_heat_by_cultivar)`. The full three-way interaction does not improve the fit, p = `r fmt_p(hc_p_three_way)`; the comparison of the candidate models is in Appendix C, together with a beta-binomial model that treats the same data directly as a proportion and gives the same ordering.


## 6) How does heat stress affect yield as measured by the percentage of healthy fruit by weight?

The second percentage measure uses weight instead of count. For each plot, `healthy_weight_prop` is the weight of healthy fruit divided by total fruit weight, so it lies between 0 and 1. A beta GLMM with a logit link is the natural model for a proportion, with a random intercept for each pair and fixed effects for heat group, cultivar and year.

### 6.1 Final model

```{r hp-fit, include=FALSE}
hp_final <- glmmTMB(
  healthy_weight_prop ~ heat_group + cultivar + year + (1 | pair_id),
  family = beta_family(link = "logit"),
  data = data
)
```

The model is

```
healthy_weight_prop ~ heat_group + cultivar + year + (1 | pair_id)
```

No plot has a share of exactly 0 or 1, so the raw proportions are used without adjustment. On the logit scale a coefficient is a change in log odds, and `exp(beta)` is the multiplicative change in the odds that a gram of harvested fruit is healthy, again against Control in 2024 for Mullica Queen.

### 6.2 Results

```{r hp-contrasts, include=FALSE}
hp_emm    <- emmeans(hp_final, ~ heat_group)
hp_emm_df <- as.data.frame(summary(hp_emm, type = "response"))
hp_resp   <- intersect(names(hp_emm_df), c("prob", "response"))[1]
hp_lo     <- intersect(names(hp_emm_df), c("asymp.LCL", "lower.CL"))[1]
hp_hi     <- intersect(names(hp_emm_df), c("asymp.UCL", "upper.CL"))[1]

hp_ct     <- contrast(hp_emm, "trt.vs.ctrl", ref = "Control", adjust = "dunnett")
hp_ct_df  <- as.data.frame(summary(hp_ct, type = "response", infer = TRUE))
hp_or     <- intersect(names(hp_ct_df), c("odds.ratio", "ratio"))[1]
hp_est    <- function(g) hp_emm_df[[hp_resp]][hp_emm_df$heat_group == g]
hp_share  <- data.frame(
  heat_group = hp_emm_df$heat_group,
  est = hp_emm_df[[hp_resp]],
  lo  = hp_emm_df[[hp_lo]],
  hi  = hp_emm_df[[hp_hi]]
)
```

```{r hp-table}
data.frame(
  `Heat group` = group_labels[as.character(hp_share$heat_group)],
  `Estimated share of healthy fruit by weight` =
    sprintf("%.1f%% (%.1f%% to %.1f%%)",
            100 * hp_share$est, 100 * hp_share$lo, 100 * hp_share$hi),
  check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL
) %>%
  kable(format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, position = "H", caption = "Estimated share of healthy fruit by weight in each heat group, averaged over cultivars and years, from the final beta model, with 95% confidence intervals.",
        longtable = FALSE)
```

```{r hp-contrast-table}
data.frame(
  Comparison = paste(group_labels[sub(" / Control", "", as.character(hp_ct_df$contrast))],
                     "vs Control"),
  `Odds ratio (95% CI)` = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f to %.2f)", hp_ct_df[[hp_or]],
                                  hp_ct_df$asymp.LCL, hp_ct_df$asymp.UCL),
  p = fmt_p(hp_ct_df$p.value),
  check.names = FALSE
) %>%
  kable(format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, position = "H", caption = "Effect of heat on the share of healthy fruit by weight, expressed as odds ratios relative to Control, adjusted for four comparisons with the same Control using Dunnett's method.",
        longtable = FALSE)
```

```{r hp-figure, fig.width=7, fig.height=3.4, fig.cap="Estimated share of healthy fruit by weight for each heat group, averaged over cultivars and years, with 95% confidence intervals. The dashed line marks the Control estimate."}
ggplot(hp_share, aes(x = heat_group, y = 100 * est)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 100 * hp_est("Control"), linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(size = 2.6, colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = 100 * lo, ymax = 100 * hi), width = 0.15,
                colour = "grey35") +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = group_labels) +
  labs(x = "Heat group", y = "Healthy fruit by weight (%)") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12)
```

Control plots keep `r fmt_share(hp_est("Control"))`% of their harvest weight as healthy fruit. Every heated group is below that, and one pulse is the lowest at `r fmt_share(hp_est("D"))`%. The four heat groups average `r fmt_share(mean(c(hp_est("D"), hp_est("C"), hp_est("B"), hp_est("A"))))`%, about `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * (hp_est("Control") - mean(c(hp_est("D"), hp_est("C"), hp_est("B"), hp_est("A")))))` percentage points below Control. The odds that a gram is healthy are `r sprintf("%.2f", hp_ct_df[[hp_or]][hp_ct_df$contrast == "A / Control"])` times the Control odds with four pulses and `r sprintf("%.2f", hp_ct_df[[hp_or]][hp_ct_df$contrast == "D / Control"])` times with one.

### 6.3 Answer

The share of healthy fruit by weight is highest in Control plots, `r fmt_share(hp_est("Control"))`%, and falls to `r fmt_share(hp_est("D"))`% with one pulse. All four heat groups sit between `r fmt_share(min(hp_share$est))`% and `r fmt_share(max(hp_share$est))`%, well below Control, and each difference is clear at p < 0.001.

The number of pulses does not order the loss. One and two pulses sit below three and four pulses, so the damage appears once the plots are heated at all rather than growing with each pulse. Year makes no difference for this measure, p = `r fmt_p(as.data.frame(joint_tests(hp_final))$p.value[3])`, while the cultivars differ.


## 7) Conclusion

Heat stress lowered both the amount and the quality of the cranberry harvest. Averaged over the four heat intensities, total fruit weight was about 12% below Control (Section 3), healthy fruit weight was `r hw_pct(hw_overall$ratio)`% below (95% CI `r hw_pct(hw_overall$upper.CL)`% to `r hw_pct(hw_overall$lower.CL)`%, Section 4), and the expected number of healthy berries was `r fewer(hc_avg_df$ratio)`% below (Section 5). Because the healthy measures fall faster than total weight, heat does not only make the crop smaller; it shifts the composition of the harvest towards rotten fruit.

The damage is concentrated in 2025. Four pulses cut total weight by about 37% and healthy weight by about 40% in that year, and cut the expected count of healthy berries by `r fewer(hc_g("A", "MQ", "2025"))`% in Mullica Queen. In 2024 the heat groups sit closer to Control and the ordering with the number of pulses is weaker. For the share of healthy fruit by weight the picture differs: Control plots keep `r fmt_share(hp_est("Control"))`% of their harvest weight as healthy fruit, one pulse is already the lowest at `r fmt_share(hp_est("D"))`%, and extra pulses do not add to the loss (Section 6). With two years of data we cannot say whether the 2025 pattern or the 2024 pattern is more typical.

Mullica Queen and Stevens differ in level more than in sensitivity. Their baselines differ by a wide margin, and the 2025 Stevens baseline is much lower than in 2024, but there is no clear evidence that the proportional effect of heat differs between the cultivars. The same proportional loss therefore costs Mullica Queen more grams.

Three limitations apply. Only the heat treatment was assigned by the experimenters, so only its effects can be read as causal. Each cultivar grew in a single field, so cultivar differences cannot be separated from field differences. With three pairs per heat group in each cultivar and year, comparisons of single heat groups are imprecise, and the models were chosen after examining the data.
