## 9) Appendix

### Appendix A: Total weight of fruit (Section 3)

#### A.1 Model specification

The final model for plot $i$ is

$$
\log(Y_i) = \mu + \alpha_{g(i)} + \beta_{t(i)} + (\alpha\beta)_{g(i)\,t(i)} + \gamma_{c(i)} + (\beta\gamma)_{t(i)\,c(i)} + b_{k(i)} + \varepsilon_i,
$$

where $Y_i$ is the total fruit weight in grams and $\log$ is the natural logarithm. $\mu$ is the overall intercept, $\alpha_{g}$ the effect of heat group $g$, $\beta_{t}$ the effect of year $t$, $\gamma_{c}$ the effect of cultivar $c$, $(\alpha\beta)_{gt}$ the heat-by-year interaction, and $(\beta\gamma)_{tc}$ the cultivar-by-year shift. $b_{k}$ is the random intercept of pair $k$, with $b_k \sim N(0, \sigma_b^2)$, and $\varepsilon_i$ is the residual error, with variance $\sigma^2_{\text{Control}}$ in Control plots and $\sigma^2_{\text{Heated}}$ in heated plots. The estimated standard deviations are $\hat\sigma_b = `r round(tw_sd_pair, 3)`$, $\hat\sigma_{\text{Control}} = `r round(tw_sd_ctrl, 3)`$ and $\hat\sigma_{\text{Heated}} = `r round(tw_sd_otc, 3)`$. The model was fitted by restricted maximum likelihood in R with nlme. The estimated coefficients are in Section 3.2.

```{r a-tw-scale, include=FALSE}
# Group SD versus group mean on the raw and the log scale
tw_grp <- data %>%
  group_by(year, cultivar, heat_group) %>%
  summarise(mean_raw = mean(total_weight),
            sd_raw   = sd(total_weight),
            mean_log = mean(log(total_weight)),
            sd_log   = sd(log(total_weight)),
            .groups = "drop")

tw_cor_raw <- cor(tw_grp$mean_raw, tw_grp$sd_raw, method = "spearman")
tw_cor_log <- cor(tw_grp$mean_log, tw_grp$sd_log, method = "spearman")
```

#### A.2 Choice of response scale and model

**Response scale.** Total weight is strictly positive and right-skewed, so the response is logged.

```{r a-tw-density, fig.width=8, fig.height=3.6, fig.cap="Total fruit weight on the raw scale (left) and the log scale (right). The raw weights are right-skewed; the log scale is closer to symmetric."}
data %>%
  transmute(`Total weight (g)` = total_weight,
            `log(total weight)` = log(total_weight)) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "scale", values_to = "value") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 20,
                 fill = "grey80", colour = "white") +
  geom_density(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ scale, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Density") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)
```

Across the 20 cells defined by cultivar, year and heat group, the Spearman correlation between the group mean and the group standard deviation is `r round(tw_cor_raw, 2)` on the raw scale and `r round(tw_cor_log, 2)` on the log scale, so the log scale gives the more even spread.

```{r a-tw-meansd, fig.width=8, fig.height=3.6, fig.cap="Group standard deviation against group mean on the raw scale (left) and the log scale (right). Each point is one cultivar, year and heat group; the line is a least-squares fit."}
tw_grp_long <- bind_rows(
  tw_grp %>% transmute(scale = "Raw scale", m = mean_raw, s = sd_raw),
  tw_grp %>% transmute(scale = "Log scale", m = mean_log, s = sd_log)
)

ggplot(tw_grp_long, aes(x = m, y = s)) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey30", size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE,
              colour = "tomato", linewidth = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ scale, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "Group mean", y = "Group SD") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)
```

Logging also makes each heat effect a ratio, so a ratio of 0.80 is 20% less fruit.

**Choosing the model.** Five models differ only in how heat enters the fixed part, and all five keep the random intercept for pair and the cultivar-by-year shift. H0 has one heat effect. H1 lets it differ by cultivar, H2 by year, and H3 includes both interactions. H4 replaces the five-level heat group by treatment by intensity, which splits the Control plots by the intensity of their paired heated plot instead of pooling them, so it tests whether pooling is justified.

The profiles below motivate the heat-by-year term: in 2024 the heat groups are close to Control, whereas in 2025 the mean falls with the number of pulses, and Stevens is much lower in 2025 than in 2024.

```{r a-tw-heat-year, fig.width=9, fig.height=4, fig.cap="Mean total fruit weight by heat group and year, separately for each cultivar. In 2024 the four heat groups are close to Control; in 2025 the mean falls with the number of pulses, and Stevens is much lower than in 2024."}
tw_summ <- data %>%
  group_by(heat_group, year, cultivar) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(total_weight),
            se = sd(total_weight) / sqrt(n()),
            .groups = "drop")

ggplot(tw_summ, aes(x = heat_group, y = mean, colour = year, group = year)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - se, ymax = mean + se), width = 0.12) +
  facet_wrap(~ cultivar, labeller = labeller(cultivar = eda_cultivar_labels)) +
  labs(x = "Heat group", y = "Mean total fruit weight (g)", colour = "Year") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)
```

The candidate fixed-effect structures are:

```{r a-tw-candidates, include=FALSE}
fit_lmm <- function(form) lmer(form, data = data, REML = FALSE)

tw_h0 <- fit_lmm(log(total_weight) ~ heat_group + cultivar + year + year:cultivar + (1 | pair_id))

tw_h1 <- fit_lmm(log(total_weight) ~ heat_group * cultivar + year + year:cultivar + (1 | pair_id))

tw_h2 <- fit_lmm(log(total_weight) ~ heat_group * year + cultivar + year:cultivar + (1 | pair_id))

tw_h3 <- fit_lmm(log(total_weight) ~ heat_group * (cultivar + year) + year:cultivar + (1 | pair_id))

tw_h4 <- fit_lmm(log(total_weight) ~ treatment * intensity_group + cultivar + year + year:cultivar + (1 | pair_id))
```

```{r a-tw-aic}
tw_models <- list(
  H0 = tw_h0,
  H1 = tw_h1,
  H2 = tw_h2,
  H3 = tw_h3,
  H4 = tw_h4
)

tw_aic_tab <- data.frame(
  Model = names(tw_models),
  df    = sapply(tw_models, function(m) attr(logLik(m), "df")),
  AIC   = sapply(tw_models, AIC)
) %>%
  mutate(dAIC = AIC - min(AIC))

kable(tw_aic_tab, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "AIC comparison for total weight (ML fits).")
```

```{r a-tw-lrt}
tw_lrt <- list(
  cult            = anova(tw_h0, tw_h1),   # does the heat effect depend on cultivar?
  year            = anova(tw_h0, tw_h2),   # does the heat effect depend on year?
  both            = anova(tw_h0, tw_h3),   # both interactions at once
  year_after_cult = anova(tw_h1, tw_h3),   # heat x year after heat x cultivar
  cult_after_year = anova(tw_h2, tw_h3)    # heat x cultivar after heat x year
)
tw_lrt

# p-values quoted in the text
tw_p_cult            <- tw_lrt$cult$`Pr(>Chisq)`[2]
tw_p_year            <- tw_lrt$year$`Pr(>Chisq)`[2]
tw_p_both            <- tw_lrt$both$`Pr(>Chisq)`[2]
tw_p_year_after_cult <- tw_lrt$year_after_cult$`Pr(>Chisq)`[2]
tw_p_cult_after_year <- tw_lrt$cult_after_year$`Pr(>Chisq)`[2]
```

H2 has the smallest AIC, so we take H2. The likelihood-ratio tests agree: heat
by year improves the fit at p = `r format.pval(tw_p_year, digits = 3, eps = 0.001)`,
heat by cultivar does not at p = `r format.pval(tw_p_cult, digits = 3, eps = 0.001)`,
and adding heat by cultivar after heat by year leaves the fit unchanged at
p = `r format.pval(tw_p_cult_after_year, digits = 3, eps = 0.001)`. H4 has a
larger AIC than H2, so the Control plots can be pooled into one Control group.

#### A.3 Residual variance and model checks

The selected model assumes one residual variance. Control and heated plots may
differ in spread, so the same fixed and random effects were refitted in nlme with
a separate residual variance for each group:

```{r a-tw-var, include=FALSE}
tw_hom <- lme(log(total_weight) ~ heat_group * year + cultivar + year:cultivar,
              random = ~ 1 | pair_id, data = data, method = "REML")
tw_het <- update(tw_hom, weights = varIdent(form = ~ 1 | treatment))

tw_var_lrt <- anova(tw_hom, tw_het)
tw_var_p <- tw_var_lrt$`p-value`[2]
```

**Residual spread.** With one residual variance the residuals of heated plots are more spread out than those of Control plots. Ignoring this would make comparisons of heated plots look more precise than they are. The likelihood-ratio test of the extra variance gives p = `r format.pval(tw_var_p, digits = 3, eps = 0.001)`, and the estimated residual standard deviation of heated plots is `r round(tw_sd_otc / tw_sd_ctrl, 1)` times that of Control plots.

```{r a-tw-resid-hom, fig.cap="Residuals against fitted values from the selected model fitted with a single residual variance for all plots. Each point is one plot; black points are Control plots and red points are heated plots. The dashed line marks zero. The residuals of heated plots are clearly more spread out than those of Control plots."}
data %>%
  mutate(fitted = fitted(tw_hom),
         resid  = resid(tw_hom)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = fitted, y = resid, colour = treatment)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Control = "grey20", OTC = "tomato"),
                      labels = c(Control = "Control", OTC = "Heated")) +
  labs(x = "Fitted value (natural log of total weight in grams)",
       y = "Residual", colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)
```

After the refit the Pearson residuals and the estimated pair effects are close to normal.

```{r a-tw-diag, fig.width=9, fig.height=3.5, fig.cap="Diagnostic plots for the final model, which allows separate residual variances for heated and Control plots. Left: standardised (Pearson) residuals against fitted values; black points are Control plots and red points are heated plots, and the dashed line marks zero. Middle: normal quantile plot of the standardised residuals. Right: normal quantile plot of the estimated pair effects. Points close to the red lines indicate approximately normal distributions."}
tw_diag_df <- data %>%
  mutate(fitted = fitted(tw_final),
         resid  = resid(tw_final, type = "pearson"))

p_resid_tw <- ggplot(tw_diag_df, aes(x = fitted, y = resid, colour = treatment)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(size = 1.8, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Control = "grey20", OTC = "tomato"),
                      labels = c(Control = "Control", OTC = "Heated")) +
  labs(x = "Fitted value (log scale)", y = "Standardised residual",
       colour = NULL, title = "Residuals vs fitted") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

p_qq_resid_tw <- ggplot(tw_diag_df, aes(sample = resid)) +
  stat_qq(colour = "grey30") +
  stat_qq_line(colour = "red") +
  labs(x = "Theoretical quantiles", y = "Standardised residual",
       title = "Residuals") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)

p_qq_pair_tw <- ggplot(data.frame(re = ranef(tw_final)[, 1]), aes(sample = re)) +
  stat_qq(colour = "grey30") +
  stat_qq_line(colour = "red") +
  labs(x = "Theoretical quantiles", y = "Estimated pair effect",
       title = "Pair effects") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)

p_resid_tw + p_qq_resid_tw + p_qq_pair_tw
```

#### A.4 Sensitivity analysis

```{r a-tw-sensitivity, include=FALSE}
tw_pct <- function(r) round(100 * (1 - r))

# Pearson residuals put Control and OTC plots on the same scale
d_res_tw <- data %>% mutate(r = resid(tw_final, type = "pearson"))

# Remove the pairs containing the three largest residuals and refit
out_pairs_tw <- d_res_tw %>% arrange(desc(abs(r))) %>% slice(1:3) %>%
  pull(pair_id) %>% as.character() %>% unique()
d_sub_tw <- data %>% filter(!pair_id %in% out_pairs_tw) %>% droplevels()

tw_sub <- update(tw_final, data = d_sub_tw)
tw_n_removed <- 2 * length(out_pairs_tw)

tw_avg <- function(model) {
  as.data.frame(summary(
    contrast(emmeans(model, ~ heat_group | year, type = "response"),
             list("OTC avg vs Control" = c(-1, 1/4, 1/4, 1/4, 1/4))),
    type = "response", infer = TRUE))
}

tw_full_avg <- tw_avg(tw_final)
tw_sub_avg  <- tw_avg(tw_sub)
tw_full_24 <- tw_full_avg[tw_full_avg$year == "2024", ]
tw_full_25 <- tw_full_avg[tw_full_avg$year == "2025", ]
tw_sub_24  <- tw_sub_avg[tw_sub_avg$year == "2024", ]
tw_sub_25  <- tw_sub_avg[tw_sub_avg$year == "2025", ]
```

We removed the `r length(out_pairs_tw)` pairs that hold the three largest
standardised residuals, `r tw_n_removed` plots in all, and refitted the final
model. The average reduction over the four heat groups is `r tw_pct(tw_sub_24$ratio)`%
in 2024 and `r tw_pct(tw_sub_25$ratio)`% in 2025, against `r tw_pct(tw_full_24$ratio)`%
and `r tw_pct(tw_full_25$ratio)`% for the full data, so the conclusions do not
depend on these plots.

### Appendix B: Healthy fruit weight (Section 4)

#### B.1 Model specification

The final model for plot $i$ is

$$
\log(Y_i) = \mu + \alpha_{g(i)} + \beta_{t(i)} + (\alpha\beta)_{g(i)\,t(i)} + \gamma_{c(i)} + (\beta\gamma)_{t(i)\,c(i)} + b_{k(i)} + \varepsilon_i,
$$

where $Y_i$ is the healthy fruit weight in grams and $\log$ is the natural logarithm. $\mu$ is the overall intercept, $\alpha_{g}$ the effect of heat group $g$, $\beta_{t}$ the effect of year $t$, $\gamma_{c}$ the effect of cultivar $c$, $(\alpha\beta)_{gt}$ the heat-by-year interaction, and $(\beta\gamma)_{tc}$ the cultivar-by-year shift. $b_{k}$ is the random intercept of pair $k$, with $b_k \sim N(0, \sigma_b^2)$, and $\varepsilon_i$ is the residual error, with variance $\sigma^2_{\text{Control}}$ in Control plots and $\sigma^2_{\text{Heated}}$ in heated plots. The estimated standard deviations are $\hat\sigma_b = `r round(sd_pair, 3)`$, $\hat\sigma_{\text{Control}} = `r round(sd_ctrl, 3)`$ and $\hat\sigma_{\text{Heated}} = `r round(sd_otc, 3)`$. The model was fitted by restricted maximum likelihood in R with nlme. The estimated coefficients are in Appendix B.4.

#### B.2 Choice of response scale and model

**Response scale.** We modelled the natural logarithm of healthy weight. On the raw scale, groups with a higher mean also varied more: the Spearman correlation between the group mean and the group standard deviation is `r round(hw_cor_raw, 2)` across the 20 cells, against `r round(hw_cor_log, 2)` on the log scale. The log scale therefore keeps the residual spread more even.

**Choosing the model.** We compared six models that differ only in how heat enters the fixed part, using likelihood-ratio tests together with AIC and BIC. Heat affects healthy weight at p `r hw_p(hw_lrt_p["heat"])`. Letting the heat effect differ between years improves the fit at p `r hw_p(hw_lrt_p["year"])`; letting it differ between cultivars does not, p `r hw_p(hw_lrt_p["cult"])`. The year-specific model also has the lowest AIC. BIC penalises extra parameters more heavily and prefers the simpler common-effect model.

The year-specific heat effect mainly changes the dose response: the slope per additional pulse differs between the two years at p `r hw_p(hw_slope_diff$p.value)`, although the overall test of a year difference is only marginal at p `r hw_p(hw_jt_hy$p.value)`.

```{r hw-model-table}
hw_model_desc <- c("No heat effect",
                   "Same heat effect in all cultivars and years",
                   "Heat effect differs between cultivars",
                   "Heat effect differs between years (selected)",
                   "Heat effect differs between cultivars and between years",
                   "Heat effect differs in every cultivar-year combination")
hw_model_cmp <- c("", "vs. model 1", "vs. model 2", "vs. model 2", "vs. model 4", "vs. model 5")
hw_model_p   <- c(NA, hw_lrt_p[c("heat", "cult", "year", "cult_after_year", "three")])

data.frame(Model       = 1:6,
           Description = hw_model_desc,
           Parameters  = hw_aic_tab$df,
           AIC         = hw_aic_tab$AIC,
           BIC         = hw_aic_tab$BIC,
           Test        = hw_model_cmp,
           p           = ifelse(is.na(hw_model_p), "",
                                ifelse(hw_model_p < 0.001, "< 0.001",
                                       sprintf("%.3f", hw_model_p)))) %>%
  kable(digits = 1, row.names = FALSE,
        col.names = c("Model", "Heat effect", "Parameters", "AIC", "BIC",
                      "Likelihood-ratio test", "p-value"),
        caption = "Candidate models for the natural logarithm of healthy fruit weight. All models include cultivar, year, the cultivar-by-year interaction and a random effect for each pair, and were fitted by maximum likelihood with a single residual variance. Parameters counts all estimated quantities, including the variances. Lower AIC and BIC indicate a better balance between fit and model size. The p-value is from a likelihood-ratio test of the model against the model named in the previous column.")
```

#### B.3 Residual variance and model checks

**Unequal variances in heated and Control plots.** When the selected model was fitted with one residual variance, the residuals of heated plots were clearly more spread out than those of Control plots. Ignoring this would understate the uncertainty of comparisons involving heated plots, so we refitted the model with separate residual variances, which fitted much better: likelihood-ratio test p `r hw_p(hw_var_lrt$"p-value"[2])`, and the estimated residual standard deviation of heated plots is about `r round(sd_otc / sd_ctrl, 1)` times that of Control plots. With this change the residuals have a similar spread in both groups, and both the residuals and the estimated pair effects are close to normal, apart from two heated plots with unusually low healthy weight, which we examine in Appendix B.5.

```{r hw-resid-lmm, fig.cap="Residuals against fitted values from the selected model fitted with a single residual variance for all plots. Each point is one plot; black points are Control plots and red points are heated plots. The dashed line marks zero. The residuals of heated plots are clearly more spread out than those of Control plots."}
data %>%
  mutate(fitted = fitted(hw_lmm),
         resid  = resid(hw_lmm)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = fitted, y = resid, colour = treatment)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Control = "grey20", OTC = "tomato"),
                      labels = c(Control = "Control", OTC = "Heated")) +
  labs(x = "Fitted value (natural log of healthy weight in grams)",
       y = "Residual", colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)
```

```{r hw-diag-final, fig.width=9, fig.height=3.5, fig.cap="Diagnostic plots for the final model, which allows separate residual variances for heated and Control plots. Left: standardised (Pearson) residuals against fitted values; black points are Control plots and red points are heated plots, and the dashed line marks zero. Middle: normal quantile plot of the standardised residuals. Right: normal quantile plot of the estimated pair effects. Points close to the red lines indicate approximately normal distributions."}
library(patchwork)

hw_diag_df <- data %>%
  mutate(fitted = fitted(hw_final),
         resid  = resid(hw_final, type = "pearson"))

p_resid <- ggplot(hw_diag_df, aes(x = fitted, y = resid, colour = treatment)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(size = 1.8, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Control = "grey20", OTC = "tomato"),
                      labels = c(Control = "Control", OTC = "Heated")) +
  labs(x = "Fitted value (log scale)", y = "Standardised residual",
       colour = NULL, title = "Residuals vs fitted") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

p_qq_resid <- ggplot(hw_diag_df, aes(sample = resid)) +
  stat_qq(colour = "grey30") +
  stat_qq_line(colour = "red") +
  labs(x = "Theoretical quantiles", y = "Standardised residual",
       title = "Residuals") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)

p_qq_pair <- ggplot(data.frame(re = ranef(hw_final)[, 1]), aes(sample = re)) +
  stat_qq(colour = "grey30") +
  stat_qq_line(colour = "red") +
  labs(x = "Theoretical quantiles", y = "Estimated pair effect",
       title = "Pair effects") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)

p_resid + p_qq_resid + p_qq_pair
```

#### B.4 Coefficients

```{r hw-coef-table}
hw_term_labels <- c(
  "(Intercept)"          = "Intercept (Control, 2024, Mullica Queen)",
  "heat_groupD"          = "1 pulse",
  "heat_groupC"          = "2 pulses",
  "heat_groupB"          = "3 pulses",
  "heat_groupA"          = "4 pulses",
  "year2025"             = "Year 2025",
  "cultivarST"           = "Stevens",
  "heat_groupD:year2025" = "1 pulse × 2025",
  "heat_groupC:year2025" = "2 pulses × 2025",
  "heat_groupB:year2025" = "3 pulses × 2025",
  "heat_groupA:year2025" = "4 pulses × 2025",
  "year2025:cultivarST"  = "2025 × Stevens"
)

data.frame(Term     = hw_term_labels[rownames(hw_coef_tab)],
           Estimate = hw_coef_tab[, "Value"],
           SE       = hw_coef_tab[, "Std.Error"],
           Ratio    = exp(hw_coef_tab[, "Value"]),
           CI       = sprintf("%.2f to %.2f",
                              exp(hw_coef_ci[, "lower"]), exp(hw_coef_ci[, "upper"])),
           p        = ifelse(hw_coef_tab[, "p-value"] < 0.001, "< 0.001",
                             sprintf("%.3f", hw_coef_tab[, "p-value"])),
           row.names = NULL) %>%
  kable(digits = c(0, 3, 3, 2, 0, 0),
        col.names = c("Term", "Estimate (log scale)", "Standard error",
                      "Ratio", "95% CI for ratio", "p-value"),
        caption = "Estimated fixed effects of the final model. Estimates are on the natural log scale; Ratio is the exponential of the estimate, i.e. the multiplicative change in healthy weight. The reference levels are Control, 2024 and Mullica Queen. For the intercept, the exponential is the estimated healthy weight in grams of Control plots of Mullica Queen in 2024. The heat group terms compare each heat group with Control in 2024; the terms marked × 2025 give the additional multiplicative change in 2025. The p-values are not adjusted for multiple comparisons.")
```

#### B.5 Sensitivity analysis

To check whether our conclusions depend on the two heated plots with unusually low healthy weight, we removed the `r length(out_pairs)` pairs that hold them, `r hw_n_removed` plots in all, and refitted the final model. The estimated effects became slightly smaller and the main conclusions did not change: the average reduction is `r hw_pct(hw_sub_avg24$ratio)`% in 2024 and `r hw_pct(hw_sub_avg25$ratio)`% in 2025, and the reduction per additional pulse in 2025 is `r hw_pct(hw_sub_slope25$ratio)`%. The only other change is that two heat groups in 2024 become individually discernible, which confirms that the evidence for them is borderline.

### Appendix C: Healthy count: model building (Section 5)

```{r a-hc-explore, fig.width=8, fig.height=3.5, fig.cap="Number of healthy berries per plot by heat group, with the mean and one standard error in red. Grey points are individual plots."}
ggplot(data, aes(x = heat_group, y = healthy_n)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.12, alpha = 0.5, colour = "grey40", size = 1.6) +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se, colour = "red", size = 0.5) +
  facet_grid(year ~ cultivar, labeller = labeller(cultivar = cultivar_labels)) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = group_labels) +
  labs(x = "Heat group", y = "Healthy berries per plot") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)
```

Counts are non-negative with a variance that grows with the mean, so a negative-binomial model is used rather than a Poisson or a normal model. The three candidate fixed-effect structures share the random intercept for pair and were fitted with maximum likelihood:

```{r a-hc-aic}
data.frame(Model = names(hc_models),
           Parameters = sapply(hc_models, function(m) attr(logLik(m), "df")),
           AIC = sapply(hc_models, AIC),
           row.names = NULL) %>%
  kable(format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, position = "H", digits = 1, caption = "Candidate models for the number of healthy berries. All models include a random intercept for each pair. Lower AIC indicates a better balance between fit and model size.",
        longtable = FALSE)
```

```{r a-hc-lrt}
data.frame(
  Comparison = c("Main effects to all two-way interactions",
                 "All two-way to all three-way interactions"),
  `Chi-square` = round(hc_lrt$Chisq[2:3], 1),
  df = hc_lrt$`Chi Df`[2:3],
  p = fmt_p(hc_lrt$`Pr(>Chisq)`[2:3]),
  check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL
) %>%
  kable(format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, position = "H", caption = "Likelihood-ratio tests between the candidate models for the number of healthy berries.",
        longtable = FALSE)
```

Adding the two-way interactions improves the fit, p `r fmt_p(hc_p_two_way)`, while adding the three-way interaction does not, p = `r fmt_p(hc_p_three_way)`, and it raises the AIC. The model with all two-way interactions is therefore used for the estimates in Section 5.

**A proportion model as a check.** The section models counts, but the measure is a percentage, so the same data were also modelled directly as a proportion. A beta-binomial GLMM was fitted to the number of healthy and rotten berries of each plot, with a logit link, the same fixed effects and the same random intercept for pair:

```{r a-hc-bb, include=FALSE}
hc_bb <- glmmTMB(cbind(healthy_n, rotten_n) ~ heat_group + cultivar + year + (1 | pair_id),
                 family = betabinomial(link = "logit"), data = data)
hc_bb_df <- as.data.frame(summary(emmeans(hc_bb, ~ heat_group), type = "response"))
hc_bb_p  <- intersect(names(hc_bb_df), c("prob", "response"))[1]
hc_bb_lo <- intersect(names(hc_bb_df), c("asymp.LCL", "lower.CL"))[1]
hc_bb_hi <- intersect(names(hc_bb_df), c("asymp.UCL", "upper.CL"))[1]
```

```{r a-hc-bb-table}
data.frame(
  `Heat group` = group_labels[as.character(hc_bb_df$heat_group)],
  `Estimated share of healthy berries by count` =
    sprintf("%.1f%% (%.1f%% to %.1f%%)",
            100 * hc_bb_df[[hc_bb_p]], 100 * hc_bb_df[[hc_bb_lo]], 100 * hc_bb_df[[hc_bb_hi]]),
  check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL
) %>%
  kable(format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, position = "H",
        caption = "Estimated share of healthy berries by count in each heat group, averaged over cultivars and years, from a beta-binomial GLMM on the healthy and rotten counts, with 95% confidence intervals.",
        longtable = FALSE)
```

The two models answer different questions. The negative-binomial model describes how many healthy berries a plot carries, while the beta-binomial model describes the share of the berries that are healthy once the total is known. Their likelihoods therefore refer to different data, so AIC cannot choose between them. On the pattern the two agree: Control keeps `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * hc_bb_df[[hc_bb_p]][hc_bb_df$heat_group == "Control"])`% of its berries healthy, every heat group is lower, and four pulses are the lowest at `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * hc_bb_df[[hc_bb_p]][hc_bb_df$heat_group == "A"])`%, which is the same ordering as the count model in Section 5.


### Appendix D: Share of healthy fruit by weight: model building (Section 6)

```{r a-hp-explore, fig.width=7.5, fig.height=3.0, fig.cap="Share of healthy fruit by weight for each plot, by heat group, with the mean and one standard error in red. The share is bounded by 0 and 1, which is why a beta model is used."}
ggplot(data, aes(x = heat_group, y = healthy_weight_prop)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.12, alpha = 0.5, colour = "grey40", size = 1.6) +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se, colour = "red", size = 0.5) +
  facet_grid(year ~ cultivar, labeller = labeller(cultivar = cultivar_labels)) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = group_labels) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * x)) +
  labs(x = "Heat group", y = "Healthy fruit by weight") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)
```

The share is a proportion bounded by 0 and 1, and its variance depends on its mean. None of the `r nrow(data)` plots sits exactly at 0 or 1; the observed shares run from about `r fmt_share(min(data$healthy_weight_prop), 0)`% to nearly 100%. A beta GLMM on the logit scale is used, with a random intercept for pair.

```{r a-hp-candidates, include=FALSE}
hp_fixed <- glmmTMB(healthy_weight_prop ~ heat_group + cultivar + year + (1 | pair_id),
                    family = beta_family(link = "logit"), data = data)
hp_noyear <- glmmTMB(healthy_weight_prop ~ heat_group + cultivar + (1 | pair_id),
                     family = beta_family(link = "logit"), data = data)

hp_year_lrt <- anova(hp_noyear, hp_fixed)
hp_p_year   <- hp_year_lrt$`Pr(>Chisq)`[2]
```

The beta-binomial model on the counts of healthy and rotten berries is an alternative way to describe the same composition, but it models a share of berries by number, not a share of weight, so its likelihood is not comparable with the beta model. The beta model on the proportion is used for the results in Section 6.

Year contributes little to the share by weight. Dropping it changes the fit by p = `r fmt_p(hp_p_year)`, so the year term is kept only so that this model has the same fixed-effect structure as the other yield models and the measures stay comparable.
